name: Voting Rights
description: A history of legislative acts, Supreme Court decisions, and federal interventions that have expanded or contracted voting access in the United States — from Reconstruction through the present.
overlay_prompt: Add your district, county, or community's voting history — redistricting events, turnout data, demographic shifts, or local legislation.
source_note: Events sourced from U.S. Supreme Court records, Congressional Research Service, NAACP Legal Defense Fund, Brennan Center for Justice, and National Archives.

entries.title: VRA Transforms Registration
entries.note: Black voter registration in Alabama went from ~19% to 51% within three years of VRA passage.

entries.title: District 7 Created
entries.note: Following the 1990 census, Alabama created its first majority-Black congressional district under VRA pressure.

entries.title: Shelby Removes Preclearance
entries.note: Alabama immediately began challenging rules previously blocked by DOJ preclearance.

entries.title: Alabama Draws Challenged Map
entries.note: Led directly to Allen v. Milligan.

entries.title: SCOTUS Orders Redraw
entries.note: Allen v. Milligan forced Alabama to create a second district where Black voters can elect a representative of their choice.

primary_sources: U.S. Department of Justice Civil Rights Division

events.title: 13th Amendment Ratified
events.description: Abolished slavery and involuntary servitude, except as punishment for crime. Laid the legal foundation for citizenship and eventual voting rights for formerly enslaved people.

events.title: 14th Amendment Ratified
events.description: Granted citizenship to all persons born or naturalized in the United States and guaranteed equal protection under the law. Became the foundational legal text for decades of civil rights litigation.

events.title: 15th Amendment Ratified
events.description: Prohibited the federal government and states from denying a citizen the right to vote based on race, color, or previous condition of servitude. Immediately undermined by poll taxes, literacy tests, and violence across the South.

events.title: Compromise of 1877 — End of Reconstruction
events.description: The political deal that ended Reconstruction and withdrew federal troops from the South. Without federal enforcement, Southern states rapidly implemented Jim Crow laws, poll taxes, literacy tests, and grandfather clauses to systematically disenfranchise Black voters.

events.title: Plessy v. Ferguson
events.description: Supreme Court upheld racial segregation under the 'separate but equal' doctrine. Entrenched the legal architecture of Jim Crow for nearly six decades and provided cover for systematic voter suppression.

events.title: 19th Amendment Ratified
events.description: Prohibited denying the right to vote based on sex. Extended suffrage to women, though Black women in the South remained effectively disenfranchised through Jim Crow mechanisms for another 45 years.

events.title: Smith v. Allwright
events.description: Supreme Court ruled that white-only primary elections in Texas violated the 15th Amendment. Struck down the 'white primary' as a mechanism for excluding Black voters from meaningful political participation in one-party Southern states.

events.title: Brown v. Board of Education
events.description: Supreme Court unanimously struck down racial segregation in public schools, overturning Plessy v. Ferguson. While primarily an education case, it fundamentally undermined the legal architecture of Jim Crow and catalyzed the broader civil rights movement.

events.title: Civil Rights Act of 1957
events.description: First federal civil rights legislation since Reconstruction. Established the Civil Rights Division of the DOJ and the Civil Rights Commission. Authorized federal prosecution of those who interfered with the right to vote. Limited in enforcement power but a significant symbolic and structural step.

events.title: 24th Amendment Ratified
events.description: Abolished the poll tax in federal elections. Poll taxes had been used since Reconstruction to prevent poor Black voters — and poor white voters — from voting. Extended to state elections by Harper v. Virginia Board of Elections in 1966.

events.title: Civil Rights Act of 1964
events.description: Landmark legislation prohibiting discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin. Title I addressed voting rights by prohibiting unequal application of voter registration requirements. Set the stage for the Voting Rights Act the following year.

events.title: Voting Rights Act of 1965
events.description: The most consequential voting rights legislation in American history. Prohibited discriminatory voting practices. Established federal oversight — the preclearance requirement — requiring states with histories of discrimination to get DOJ approval before changing any voting law. Directly produced dramatic increases in Black voter registration across the South within years of passage.

events.title: South Carolina v. Katzenbach
events.description: Supreme Court unanimously upheld the constitutionality of the Voting Rights Act, including its preclearance provisions. Confirmed Congress had broad authority under the 15th Amendment to combat voting discrimination. The ruling that Shelby County v. Holder would effectively reverse 47 years later.

events.title: 26th Amendment Ratified
events.description: Lowered the voting age from 21 to 18. Passed during the Vietnam War era amid the argument that citizens old enough to be drafted should be old enough to vote. Added approximately 11 million new eligible voters.

events.title: VRA Reauthorization & Amendment
events.description: Congress reauthorized the Voting Rights Act for 25 years and amended Section 2 to establish a results-based test for voting discrimination — meaning plaintiffs no longer needed to prove discriminatory intent, only discriminatory effect. A significant strengthening of the VRA's enforcement reach.

events.title: Thornburg v. Gingles
events.description: Supreme Court established the legal standard for when at-large or multimember electoral systems violate Section 2 of the VRA by diluting minority voting strength. Created the 'Gingles test' — three preconditions plaintiffs must establish to prove vote dilution. Became the foundational framework for majority-minority district litigation.

events.title: National Voter Registration Act
events.description: Required states to offer voter registration opportunities at DMVs and public assistance agencies, and through mail-in registration. Significantly reduced registration barriers and expanded the electorate.

events.title: Shaw v. Reno
events.description: Supreme Court ruled that a North Carolina congressional district drawn to create a majority-Black district was subject to strict scrutiny under the Equal Protection Clause. First major ruling that racial gerrymandering — even when designed to increase minority representation — could be unconstitutional if race was the predominant factor.

events.title: Miller v. Johnson
events.description: Supreme Court extended Shaw v. Reno, ruling that Georgia's majority-Black congressional district was unconstitutional because race was the predominant factor in its creation. Established that strict scrutiny applies whenever race is the dominant and controlling rationale in drawing district lines.

events.title: Bush v. Gore
events.description: Supreme Court halted the Florida recount in the 2000 presidential election, effectively deciding the outcome. The per curiam opinion stated it should not serve as precedent. Raised fundamental questions about equal protection in vote counting and the Court's role in electoral disputes.

events.title: Help America Vote Act
events.description: Passed in response to the 2000 election crisis. Required states to replace punch card and lever voting systems, established minimum election administration standards, created the Election Assistance Commission, and required provisional ballots for voters whose registration was in question.

events.title: VRA Reauthorized for 25 Years
events.description: Congress reauthorized the Voting Rights Act for another 25 years with overwhelming bipartisan support — 390-33 in the House, 98-0 in the Senate. President Bush signed it. The preclearance provisions were retained and strengthened. Seven years later, the Supreme Court would gut them.

events.title: Crawford v. Marion County Election Board
events.description: Supreme Court upheld Indiana's strict photo ID requirement for voting, finding it did not impose an unconstitutional burden on the right to vote. Opened the door for states to enact strict voter ID laws. Disproportionate impact on Black, Latino, elderly, and low-income voters documented in subsequent research.

events.title: Shelby County v. Holder
events.description: The most consequential rollback of voting rights since Reconstruction. Supreme Court struck down Section 4(b) of the VRA — the formula used to determine which states required preclearance — rendering Section 5 unenforceable. Within hours of the ruling, states began implementing voting changes that had previously been blocked by the DOJ. Texas announced a voter ID law. North Carolina passed sweeping voting restrictions within weeks.

events.title: North Carolina Omnibus Voting Restrictions
events.description: Within weeks of Shelby County, North Carolina passed HB 589 — one of the most sweeping voting restriction packages in the country. Eliminated same-day registration, reduced early voting by a week, ended pre-registration for 16 and 17-year-olds, and imposed strict photo ID requirements. A federal appeals court later found the law targeted Black voters 'with almost surgical precision.'

events.title: Texas Voter ID Law (SB 14)
events.description: Texas implemented one of the strictest voter ID laws in the country within hours of the Shelby County ruling. Previously blocked by DOJ preclearance. Required one of seven specific forms of photo ID. Concealed carry permits accepted; student IDs from state universities were not.

events.title: Evenwel v. Abbott
events.description: Supreme Court unanimously ruled that states may use total population — not just eligible voter population — as the basis for drawing legislative districts. Preserved the political representation of communities with large non-citizen populations, particularly Latino communities in Texas.

events.title: 4th Circuit: NC Targeted Black Voters
events.description: The 4th Circuit Court of Appeals struck down North Carolina's 2013 voting restriction law, finding that it targeted African American voters 'with almost surgical precision.' The court found the legislature had requested racial data on voting practices and then restricted those practices disproportionately used by Black voters.

events.title: Husted v. A. Philip Randolph Institute
events.description: Supreme Court upheld Ohio's voter roll purge process, which removed voters who had not voted in two years and failed to respond to a confirmation notice. Critics argued the process disproportionately removed legitimate voters — particularly in minority and low-income communities. Green-lit aggressive voter roll purges nationwide.

events.title: Rucho v. Common Cause
events.description: Supreme Court ruled 5-4 that federal courts cannot review partisan gerrymandering claims — that such claims present political questions beyond the reach of federal courts. Effectively handed states unlimited authority to draw maps favoring the party in power, with no federal judicial remedy.

events.title: Brnovich v. Democratic National Committee
events.description: Supreme Court upheld two Arizona voting restrictions and significantly narrowed the scope of Section 2 of the VRA. Created a new multi-factor test that makes it harder to challenge voting restrictions under the VRA. Substantially weakened the last major enforcement mechanism of the Voting Rights Act.

events.title: John Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act — Stalled
events.description: Legislation designed to restore and strengthen the Voting Rights Act following Shelby County, including a new preclearance formula. Passed the House but failed to overcome a Senate filibuster. Named for the late congressman and civil rights leader who was beaten on the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma in 1965.

events.title: Allen v. Milligan
events.description: Supreme Court ruled 5-4 that Alabama's congressional map illegally diluted Black voting power in violation of Section 2 of the VRA, rejecting Alabama's argument that race-neutral redistricting principles precluded drawing a second majority-Black district. A significant — and unexpected — ruling that preserved Section 2 as an enforcement tool.

events.title: Alexander v. South Carolina State Conference of the NAACP
events.description: Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that South Carolina's congressional map was not an unconstitutional racial gerrymander, reversing a lower court finding. Significantly raised the evidentiary bar plaintiffs must clear to prove racial gerrymandering — requiring challengers to disentangle race from partisanship even when the two are tightly correlated. Made it substantially easier for states to use race as a proxy for partisan advantage.
